Q: Something is wrong with git restore a renamed file A:

git restore restores the working tree from the index by default, not from HEAD. That is the key to both of your observations. The manual is explicit about the default source:

By default, if --staged is given, the contents are restored from HEAD,otherwise from the index. Use --source to restore from a different commit.

— git-restore(1), DESCRIPTION

Why the file does not come back after git mv

When you run git mv file.1 file.1st, git updates the index in one step:

  • file.1 is removed from the index (staged deletion)

  • file.1st is added to the index (staged addition, shown as a rename)

So after git mv, the index no longer contains a file.1 entry at all:


git status
# renamed: file.1 -> file.1st   (staged)

Now git restore file.1 means "write the index's file.1 state into the worktree". Because the index has no file.1 entry, there is nothing to write, and the file stays missing. The same manual section also says:

If a path is tracked but does not exist in the restore source, it will be removed to match the source.

— git-restore(1), DESCRIPTION

Restoring from the index (where file.1 is gone) therefore removes it from the worktree — the opposite of what you wanted.

Why it is not untracked either

The untracked status only applies to files that exist in the worktree but are not present in the index and not ignored (see the [gitglossary(7)definition of "untracked"](https://git-scm.com/docs/gitglossary#def_untracked_file)).A file restored from the index is, by definition, tracked again — it matches the index, so git status shows nothing for it. Untracked never comes fromgit restore; it comes from a brand-new file git has never seen.

How to actually get the file back

Restore the worktree from HEAD (the last committed version) instead of from the index:


git restore --source=HEAD --worktree file.1
# or the classic form:
git checkout HEAD -- file.1

The git-checkout(1) manual documentsthe equivalent form:

git checkout <tree-ish> [--] <pathspec>... — Replace the specified filesand/or directories with the version from the given commit or tree and addthem to the index. For example, git checkout main file.txt will replacefile.txt with the version from main.

— git-checkout(1)

--source=HEAD points git restore at the last committed version, which still contains file.1.

If you also want to undo the staged rename (so file.1st stops being staged), reset the index first with git reset — per git-reset(1),the default --mixed mode "updates the index to match the new HEAD, so nothing will be staged" while leaving the working tree unchanged:


git reset            # unstage everything (--mixed is the default)
git restore file.1   # now the index still has file.1 -> restores it

Why the git add-only case "works"

When you git add file.1 but do not commit, the index does containfile.1. Deleting the worktree file then leaves a "deleted" entry in the index, so git restore file.1 has an index entry to restore from — which is why it behaves as you expect. The difference is entirely whether the index still holds the path.

Verifying the fix

git mv file.1 file.1st          # reproduce
git status                      # renamed: file.1 -> file.1st
git restore --source=HEAD --worktree file.1
ls file.1                       # file.1 is back
git status                      # file.1 matches index? shows staged rename or clean

Q: Character offset in Brat's annotation file through python A:

The problem comes from the fact the carriage returns (\r in the text file) and newline (\n) are not considered the same way in Windows and Unix/Mac. If you use a Windows system to generate or modify the .txt files there will be some '\r\n' but brat (that is not thought for Windows) will only counts the '\n' sign.

Using python, you may pass from Windows count to brat count using a dict after having opened the file with the argument newline='' that ensures '\r' will be present in the created W_Contents variable:

with open('file.txt', newline='', encoding='utf-8') as f:
    W_Content = f.read()

counter = -1
UfromW_dic = {}
for n, char in enumerate(W_Content):
    if char != '\r':
        counter += 1
        UfromW_dic[n] = counter

After that, the intial span [x,y] will be found at [UfromW_dic[x],UfromW_dic[y]].

Q: Converting from XML annotations to BRAT format A:

In case someone still needs an answer to this question, here is a solution.

Let's say an XML file sample.xml has the following structure:

<root>
<p n='1'>Hi, my name is <fname>Mickey</fname> <lname>Mouse</lname>, and what about yourself?</p>
<p n='2'>Nice meeting you, <fname>Mickey</fname>! I am <fname>Minnie</lname>!</p>
</root>

Here is a Python solution:

# leave empty if there are no tags that should not be interpreted as named entities; or add more
ignoretags = ['root', 'p']

# dictionary, in case some named entities have to be mapped; or just a list of tags that represent NEs
replacetags = {
    "fname": "PERS",
    "lname": "PERS"
}

# read content
content = open('sample.xml', encoding='utf-8').read()

# output files for BRAT: txt and annotations
f_txt = open('sample.txt', 'w')
f_ann = open('sample.ann', 'w')

# from txt file remove NE tags
clean_content = content
for replacetag in replacetags:
    clean_content = clean_content.replace('<{}>'.format(replacetag), '')
    clean_content = clean_content.replace('</{}>'.format(replacetag), '')

# write content to file
f_txt.write(clean_content)

# char by char
n = len(content)
i = - 1

# token id
tid = 0
# other - for output
start = -1
end = - 1
token = None
tag = None

# let's start parsing! character by character
skipped_chars = 0
number_of_tags = 0

token_buffer = ''
while i < n - 1:

    i += 1
    c = content[i]

    # beginning of an entity
    if c == '<':

    # probably the most important part: always track the count of skipped characters
        start = i - skipped_chars

        # get name of the entity
        tag_buffer = ''
        i += 1
        while content[i] != '>':
            tag_buffer += content[i]
            i += 1
        tag = tag_buffer

    # skip tags that are not NEs
        if tag not in replacetags:
            continue

        # get entity itself
        ent_buffer = ''
        i += 1
        while content[i] != '<':
            ent_buffer += content[i]
            i += 1
        token = ent_buffer

    # determine positions
        end = start + len(token)
        number_of_tags += 1

    # <fname></fname> i.e. 1 + len('fname') + 1 + 1 + 1 + len('fname') + 1
        skipped_chars += 1 + len(tag) + 1 + 1 + 1 + len(tag) + 1
        tid += 1

    # write annotation
        f_ann.write('T{}\t{} {} {}\t{}\n'.format(tid, replacetags[tag], start, end, token))

        # navigate to the end of the entity span, e.g. go behind <fname>...</fname>
        i += 1 + len(tag) + 1

Content of sample.txt

<root>
<p n='1'>Hi, my name is Mickey Mouse, and what about yourself?</p>
<p n='2'>Nice meeting you, Mickey! I am Minnie!</p>
</root>

Content of sample.ann:

T1  PERS 31 37  Mickey
T2  PERS 38 43  Mouse
T3  PERS 101 107    Mickey
T4  PERS 114 120    Minnie

And visually in BRAT:

A minor tweak would be needed in case of attributes (I added another key 'att' in replacetags dictionary, i.e. a pair would be then "fname": {"tag": "PERS", "att": "value of attribute"} and then an additional line would be written in case of tag that has attribute.

Hope someone will find this helpful!

Q: What is the practical difference between `git rm --cached`, `git reset --` and `git reset HEAD` to unstage changes? A:

git reset is the proper way to unstage, now here's why:

First let's clarify a few things: If no commit is provided git defaults commit to HEAD

git reset == git reset HEAD

As for the -- it expects a path after it.

Now, for the difference between:

git reset --mixed AND git rm --cached

(reset defaults to --mixed)

git reset --mixed
           Resets the index but not the working tree (i.e., the changed files are preserved but not marked for
           commit) and reports what has not been updated. This is the default action.

git rm --cached
       Use this option to unstage and remove paths only from the index. Working tree files, whether modified or
       not, will be left alone.

Essentially the difference being here, git rm --cached actually puts specified files into untracked, and stages their removal for the next commit. Git reset --mixed, on the other hand, simply moves the file into 'unstaged', but keeps its old version in repo.

Q: Dataframe sorting and column count A:

Use .size().reset_index(name='Count') instead of .agg({'CoffeeType':'count'}), and convert the DayOfWeek column into a categorical type with a custom Monday-to-Sunday order.

import pandas as pd

# Define the correct order for days of the week
day_order = ['Monday', 'Tuesday', 'Wednesday', 'Thursday', 'Friday', 'Saturday', 'Sunday']

# Convert DayOfWeek to a categorical type with that order
coffee_dataset['DayOfWeek'] = pd.Categorical(
    coffee_dataset['DayOfWeek'], 
    categories=day_order, 
    ordered=True
)

# Group, count, rename the column, and sort by the custom order
result = (
    coffee_dataset.groupby(['DayOfWeek', 'CoffeeType'], observed=False)
    .size()
    .reset_index(name='Count')
    .sort_values(['DayOfWeek', 'CoffeeType'])
)

print(result)
